sections.heading: Nalanda Museum
sections.content: The museum established in 1971 has a small but beautiful collection of Buddhist and Hindu bronzes and a good collection of ancient manuscripts and Buddhist statues. The manuscripts kept here were found during the excavation of the area and many of them are rare in appearance and style. The museum also displays artifacts of the Maurya, Gupta and other periods. Two enormous terracotta jars of the first century stand intact behind the museum in a shade. The collection includes copper plates and stone inscriptions, coins, pottery and samples of burnt rice (twelfth century CE) found among the ruins here.

sections.heading: Bihar- Monument- Sasaram
sections.content: Sher Shah Suri of the Suri dynasty of Bihar fought with Humayun in Delhi. His mausoleum was built in the middle of a lake in Sasaram by his architect, Aliwal Khan. The tomb is an imposing structure of stone standing and rising from a large stone terrace. This terrace rests obliquely on a platform with a flight of steps leading to the waters edge. The upper terrace is enclosed by a battlemented parapet wall with octagonal domed chambers at four corners. In the middle of the upper terrace stands the building of the mausoleum on a large octagonal chamber surrounded by a wide verandah on all the four sides. Internally, the verandah is covered by a series of 24 small domes. The roof is a pillared cupola adorned by panels of white glazed tiles now much discoloured. The interior of the tomb is sufficiently well ventilated and lighted through large windows on the top portion of the walls fitted with stone jali in varying patterns. The jambs and spandrils of the arch of the mihrab on the western wall were once profusely adorned with verses from the Quran and inscriptions, with glazed tiles of various colours arranged in geometrical patterns and with beautiful floral carvings in stone enclosed in enamel borders. Much of this decoration has already vanished.

sections.heading: Bihar- Monument- Rajgir
sections.content: Rajgir, known earlier as Rajagriha or Girivaraja, located in the rocky hills is significant for the teachings of both Buddha and Mahavira. Rajgir is 10km south of Nalanda and sacred to the memory of the founder of both Buddhism and Jainism. Lord Buddha spent many months of retreat during the rainy season here, and used to meditate and preach on Giddhkuta, the Hill of the Vultures. Lord Mahavir spent fourteen years of his life at Rajgir and Nalanda. It was in Rajgriha that Lord Buddha delivered some of his famous sermons and converted a number of people to Buddhism including King Bimbisara of Magadha. Today, Rajgir is a picturesque and serene place, visited by pilgrims from all over. Venuvana is the site of the monastery Venuvana Vihar built by King Bimbisara for Lord Buddha to reside. This was the King's first offering to Lord Buddha. Swarna Bhandar are cave chambers which were hollowed out of a single massive rock. One of the chambers is believed to have been the guard room, the rear wall has two straight vertical lines and one horizontal line cut into the rock; this doorway is supposed to lead to King Bimbisaras treasury. Inscriptions in the Sankhalipi or shell script, etched into the wall and so far undeciphered, are believed to give the clue to open the doorway. The treasure, according to folklore, is still intact. The second chamber bears a few traces of seated and standing guards etched into the outer wall.

sections.heading: Bihar- Monument - Vaishali
sections.content: Vaishali is significant to both Buddhists and Jains. Lord Buddha visited Vaishali more than once during his lifetime. He preached his last sermon here and announced his approaching Mahaparinirvana to his followers. Hundred years after he attained Mahaparinirvana, it was the venue of the second Buddhist council held at the time of king Kalasoka. Two stupas were erected to commemorate this event. Lord Mahavir was born on the outskirts Vaishali at a place called Kundupur in 527 BCE and lived in there till he was 22. Vaishali remains an important pilgrimage for Buddhists and Jains.To commemorate the importance of the site, Emperor Ashoka erected one of his famous pillars. It is made of a highly polished single piece of red sandstone, surmounted by bell shaped capital. A life-size figure of a lion surmounts the top of the pillar. There are some important Stupas here. The Buddha Stupa-I has a plain surface.The exterior of this stupa is now in a dilapidated condition One-eighth of the sacred ashes of the Lord Buddha were enshrined here in a stone casket. Excavation at this site in 1958 led to the discovery of Buddha Stupa-II with remains of another casket containing the ashes of the Lord Buddha.

sections.heading: Bihar- Monument- Bodhgaya
sections.content: The founder of Buddhism, Gautama Buddha, attained enlightenment under the sacred Bodhi tree or Banyan tree at Bodhgaya. Bodhgaya is one of the four most sacred pilgrimages for the Buddhists. The other three sacred places of Buddhists are Lumbini (Buddha's place of birth), Sarnath (the site of his first sermon) and Kushinagar (place where he left his body). Buddhists from all over the world visit the holy site of Bodhgaya. They have also built many Buddhist temples at Bodhgaya. The Mahabodhi Temple is located where Lord Buddha got enlightenment. The present Mahabodhi temple was restored around 1880 CE. Besides the main Mahabodhi temple there are several other temples at the place. In the inner sanctuary of the temple there is a huge statue of Lord Buddha. In the center of the temple there is a Shivalinga that was installed around 860 CE. It was under the Bodhi tree that Buddha attained enlightenment. A sapling of the original banyan tree was carried by Ashoka's daughter Sanghamitra to Sri Lanka and planted at Anuradhapura where it exists even now. A cutting from the Bodhi tree of Anuradhapura was planted at Bodhgaya when the original tree died. Vajrasana (the seat of stability) under the bodhi tree is believed to be the same seat where Buddha sat, during his meditation. The stone platform, under the Bodhi tree symbolizes the Vajrasana.

sections.heading: Bihar- Monument- Barabar Hill
sections.content: The Lomas Rishi Cave was a unique architectural development during Emperor Ashoka (third Cen BCE). sections.heading: Patna Museum
sections.content: Established in 1917, Patna Museum has an excellent collection of stone and terracotta sculptures especially from the Mauryan period. Didarganj Yakshi,carved out of a yellowish sand stone, is the most noteworthy piece in the museum. The sculpture is over 2,000 years old, having a lustrous finish. Mother goddess figures, clay toy animals, figurines of women, couples and deities, Chinese paintings, Thangkas and early Buddhist figures, including a standing Buddha and Bodhisattvas, made of bronzes are the other artifacts on display. Keywords-Patna Museum, Didarganj Yakshi, Mother Goddess, Thangkas.

sections.heading: Interesting Fact
sections.content: Regarded as one of the finest example of Indian art, this 5'4" tall sculpture of Ashokan period, the Didarganj Yakshi is carved out of a single piece of stone. The prominent breasts, the narrow waist, the creases on the lower abdomen, and broad hips, are classic features of feminine beauty of all ages. They show the painstaking attention to details by the artisans and especially the glossy polish. Equally striking is the depiction of clothes with which her body is draped. Elegantly folded and pleated in the front, held in place by exquisite waist ornaments (kamar-bandh).

sections.heading: Mithila Paintings
sections.content: Mithila paintings now better known as Madhubani paintings are an indigenous art form from the Mithila region of north Bihar. Here the women of the village paint figures from themes as varied as the daily life of the people to nature, religion and mythology on village walls to mark the seasonal festivals, special events and marriages. These intricately prepared designed wall paintings are passed on by a mother to her daughter. They are characterized by line drawings based on mythological themes, in bright colours and decorative borders. Traditionally Madhubani paintings were always made with Natural dyes. Black was obtained by mixing soot with cow dung, yellow from turmeric or pollen or lime and the milk of banyan . leaves; blue from indigo, red from the kusam flower juice or red sandalwood; green from the leaves of the wood apple tree; white from rice powder; orange from palasha flowers. Women of this village have been practicing this art form for centuries but it came to the forefront only in the 1960s, when a drought hit the area and people had to think of an alternative non-agricultural source of earning. Selling these traditional paintings on handmade paper was the best alternative. And today they are one of the most celebrated arts of the world.

sections.heading: Sujini embroidery
sections.content: The Sujini is a traditional quilt made in Bihar. Old clothes are used for the inner stuffing and threads drawn from the saree border are used for the embriodery. The embroidery is done in running stitch and depicts village scenes such as bride in palanquin, dancing peacocks, boy flying kite, etc. Durga depicted in sombre brown, ochre and black is another favourite imagery. The applique work of Bihar is called Khatwa and is used to craft decorative tents, canopies, shamianas, etc. The applique designs for tents are Persian type trees, flowers, animals, birds, etc.

sections.heading: Woodcraft
sections.content: Wood inlay is done with different materials, metal, ivory and stag-horn. Apart from decorative pieces like wall hangings, table tops, trays, a number of utility articles are also ornamented with inlay work. The designs are mostly geometrical, very fine and colourful.

sections.heading: Bihar  Handicrafts -Lacquerware
sections.content: Lac has been gathered and used in Bihar for ages. The vermilion container called sindurdan used in marriages by brides is made by a community called laheris. The boxes are decorated with the set motifs of fish, chakra and peacock which have a moving rythmic quality. Bangles of lac decorated with beads and glass are commercially produced in Bihar.

sections.heading: Stonecraft
sections.content: The ancient sculptures of the Mauryan period are witness to Bihar's rich heritage of stonecraft. An outstanding example is the famous Asoka pillar at Sarnath. The most noted stoneware centre of Bihar is Patharkatti in Gaya district. This area is famous for the blue black pot stone from which images and household articles like the pestle or the mortar kharal (medicine grinder) are made. Buddhist sculptures are also made out of this stone. Chandil and Karaikalla in Singhbum district and Dumka in Santhal parganas are famous for the beautifully grained greenish black soapstone.

sections.heading: Bihar  Handicrafts -Masks
sections.content: Masks are used for the Chhou dance of Saraikela in Bihar. The Masks are not only very stylish but also equally delicate. The most distinguishing features of the masks are the stylized arch-like eyebrows and elongated half closed eyes. The stylized gestures of the eyebrows, eyes and mouth are painstakingly painted to bring out the distinctive character. These features impart a sense of mystery to the mask. Traditionally only those people who were dancers were permitted to make the masks. Originally they were made of wood, later of bamboo, then pumpkin shells and now papier-mâché. These masks are painted mainly with flat transparent shades and the lines are bold and clear. Avoiding the realistic identification the masks take up a symbolic character.

sections.heading: Bihar  Handicrafts - Printed Textiles
sections.content: Printing is done on cotton, wool and silk at Bhagalpur, Bihar Sharif, Darbhanga, and Patna. Gaya, being a famous place of pilgrimage has the religious textiles with the names or footprints of deities printed all over in ochre or red. The chunris of Bihar have designs ranging from traditional to floral and animal forms. There is a small printing sector in North Bihar at Sursand where only mica (khari) printing is done. Bright colours are used and largely dots and stars strewn all over form the designs.

sections.heading: Bihar - Fair and Festivals - Chhath Puja
sections.content: Dedicated to the worship of the Sun God, Chhath is also known as Suryashashti. The word Chhath denotes the number six and thus the festival begins on the sixth day of the Hindu month of Kartik, corresponding to late October and mid November, depending on the year. The devotees take a dip, preferably in the holy river Ganges, observe a fast for the whole day and the offerings are made to the setting sun. Chhath Puja is an elaborate festival noted for its remarkable display of colorful dresses, cuisine, music, singing and extravagant rituals.

sections.heading: Bihar - Fair and Festivals - Rajgir Dance Festival
sections.content: The colourful festival of dance and music, is held at Rajgir, the ancient capital of the Magadha kings. During the festival the instrumental music, devotional songs, opera, folk dance, ballet or the other schools of classical dance and music, geniuses in their own realms of accomplishments, create an almost ethereal atmosphere to thrill true devotees. Nalanda, situated at a distance of 90 km. south east of Patna has ruins of the great ancient university and monastery. It was here that the world's first seat of higher learning, a university was established during the Gupta period. There are many versions of what the term Nalanda means. Nalam means lotus and da means to give. Both combined together, Nalanda means giver of lotus. Since Lotus is supposed to represent knowledge, Nalanda means giver of knowledge. The ruins extend over a large area and represent only a part of the extensive establishment. Nalanda has a very ancient history. It was frequently visited by Lord Vardhamana Mahavir and Lord Buddha in the 6th century BC. Nalanda was the largest residential centre of learning that the world had ever known. The library was located in a nine storied building. Since the time of Buddha, the bhikkus were always encouraged to study the various arts and sciences. Learning was greatly encouraged as it served dual proposes: knowledge and practice. The monks therefore took to learning so that they might practice it and realise Dhamma perfectly and thereby enrich the masses. Nalanda was a flourishing residential university with over 10,000 students and 1500 teachers. The university was marked by a lofty wall and one gate. Hiuen Tsang, the Chinese pilgrim spent three years at Nalanda in seventh century. He has left a detailed note about the university, its curriculum, activities and other accounts. The Tibetan pilgrim Dharmasvamin was here in 1234 and has left a gripping account of the monastery's destruction by the Muslims. The great stupa flanked by flights of steps and terraces, votive stupas and beautiful sculptures gives the glimpse of the past glory that once was Nalanda. Many of the stupas were two or the other on the same spot. The excavation of the Nalanda University archaeological complex shows that the edifices are of red brick and the gardens are beautiful. The buildings are divided by a central walkway that goes south to north, the monasteries or Viharas are east of this central alley and the temples of Chaityas to the west. The Vihara-1 is perhaps the most interesting with its cells on two floors built around a central courtyard where steps lead up to what must have been a dais for the professors to address their students. A small chapel still retains a half broken statue of the Lord Buddha. The enormous pyramidal mass of the temple no.3 is impressive and from its top commands a splendid view of the entire area. It is surrounded by smaller stupas, many of which are studded with small and big statues of the Lord Buddha in various poses or mudras.
